messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Caleb is a 30-year-old carpenter from rural Ohio, married for four years, who presented for intake following a significant deterioration in his daily functioning over the past eighteen months. He scored 61 on the PCL-5, placing him firmly in the severe range, and described himself during the first session as a man who no longer recognises himself.

The event that precipitated his current difficulties occurred on a job site approximately two years ago. Caleb and a small crew were framing a residential addition when a coworker — a man he had known for years — fell from scaffolding and landed badly on exposed rebar. Caleb was the first to reach him. He remembers the specific warmth and wetness of his colleague's blood on his hands as he tried to apply pressure to the wound, the particular metallic taste in the air that he later realised had entered his mouth when he shouted for someone to call 911, and the sight of a deep laceration across the man's abdomen that he could not look away from and cannot stop seeing. His colleague survived, but Caleb has never been able to describe the event in any coherent sequence. When asked to recount what happened, his speech fragments, he loses the thread, and he eventually shakes his head — the experience sits in him not as a story but as a cluster of sensations that resist language.

The triggers that now govern Caleb's days map precisely onto those moments of contact. Physical touch — a handshake, his wife resting her hand on his arm, even the grain of rough lumber against his palm — can instantly collapse the distance between the present and the site, flooding him with the full sensory weight of that afternoon: the heat, the smell, the sound of his own voice. A particular taste, something metallic or iron-edged that occasionally appears in food or drink, does the same, arriving without announcement and pulling him entirely out of the room he is standing in. And visible injuries on others — a cut on a coworker's hand, a bruise on his wife's leg — are almost unbearable; when these appear at work, Caleb has found himself freezing mid-task, unable to continue, the memory returning not as recollection but as reliving, completely real across every sense at once.

When these intrusions hit, Caleb has developed a set of responses that he experiences as necessary, though he is dimly aware they are not helping. He eats — sometimes large amounts of whatever is available — not from hunger but because the sensation of fullness seems to interrupt the intrusion, grounding him in his body in a way that momentarily dulls the reactivation. He has also learned to blank out deliberately, a kind of willed dissociation he describes as "going somewhere else," which he reaches for especially when the reliving is most intense. Both strategies pull him briefly back from the edge, but in the hours that follow he is left feeling disgusted with himself and more convinced than ever that he is broken. The overeating and the deliberate detachment have become, in his mind, evidence of a man who cannot manage himself — and that evidence feeds directly into the belief, now deeply held, that he has been permanently changed for the worse, that the trauma has destroyed the life he was building, and that he cannot rely on himself to be the husband or worker he once was.

These appraisals have begun to function as triggers in their own right. When Caleb thinks of himself as permanently damaged, the thought seems to summon the memory — as though the belief and the event are stored together, each one unlocking the other. And the memory, when it returns, confirms the belief so completely that he has stopped trying to argue with it. He has also, over months, narrowed his physical world: he avoids touching anything he does not have to touch, eats alone when possible to control what flavours he encounters, and turns away when anyone on site is injured. At work, this last habit has become conspicuous — his foreman has noticed that Caleb leaves the area whenever there is even a minor accident, and a conversation about his reliability has already happened once.

What finally brought Caleb in was his wife telling him, quietly and without anger, that she missed being able to touch him. He is most afraid that she is right — that the man she married is simply gone.
